title: Eternity
synopsis: You died, gently, on a Tuesday. The afterlife is a tasteful hotel with seven days to decide who you want to spend eternity with — your husband of fifty years, or the love you lost at twenty-three.

nodes.text: The carpet is deep enough to swallow a dropped ring, and the music has been sanded down until it cannot possibly offend anyone. A clerk in a cream blazer slides a folder across the desk: Your Eternity, in gold, faintly embossed. Your hands are the hands you had at thirty. Your shoes do not pinch anywhere. He clears his throat and says you have seven days to decide.

choices.text: Ask for the rules in plain English
choices.consequence: You ask him to drop the brochure voice, and he does, and the plain version is worse. Clarity in this building is not a comfort. It is a countdown with better manners.

choices.text: Ask who's waiting for you
choices.consequence: You skip the terms and go straight for the names, the way you always read the last page of a novel first. Two, he says, and lets the number sit on the desk between you.

nodes.text: One person to share forever with, he says. It must be somebody who loved you and stayed waiting, and that condition does most of the choosing before you get anywhere near it. Most people take a spouse. A surprising number take a parent. Some go on alone, which is permitted and which he does not recommend. He checks the folder again. Two are waiting for you, he says.

choices.text: Decide to meet both of them
choices.consequence: You ask to see both of them, and something in the clerk's shoulders comes down half an inch. He had been afraid you would choose fast. Now you have to earn it instead.

choices.text: Decide quickly — your husband, of course
choices.consequence: You say Henry's name inside a second, out of fifty years of habit, and hear how automatic it sounded in a quiet room. The clerk waits. You take it back before he writes anything.

nodes.text: He opens the folder where you can see it. Two lines of handwriting. Henry, who stood at your grave yesterday with his hat in both hands and could not get the words out in front of the family. And David, who promised you an entire life on a February porch and then died on a wet road at twenty-three, three months before a wedding you had half planned.

choices.text: See Henry first
choices.consequence: You pick the man whose snoring you could identify in a crowded room. Familiarity gets to go first, which is already a kind of verdict, and you know it while you say it.

choices.text: See David first
choices.consequence: You ask for the boy first and feel it land as a small betrayal, which tells you something about yourself you would rather not have learned standing in a lobby.

nodes.text: He is the Henry of your twenties: straight back, ridiculous confidence, the laugh that did the damage in the first place. But all fifty years are in him at once. He knows how you take your tea in November as opposed to July. He still tells the story about the ferry wrong. He still finishes your sentences badly and looks pleased with himself about it afterwards.

choices.text: Embrace him without speaking
choices.consequence: You reach him without saying anything and he smells like the good coat, the one you kept in a bag. Whatever you say next, the true thing has already been said.

choices.text: Ask him if he knows about David
choices.consequence: You ask, and his face does something small and quick before the smile comes back over it. He knows. He has known for fifty years and never once made you carry knowing it.

nodes.text: He is twenty-three and will never be twenty-four. He is reading the paperback that was in his jacket that night, the one with the corner turned down at page ninety. When he looks up, the smile is exactly the smile: the one you kept going on for a full year afterwards, and then eventually, quietly, stopped being able to picture at all.

choices.text: Hug him and weep
choices.consequence: You put your face into a shoulder you buried and cry until your ribs ache, and he says nothing clever, which is new. He has had fifty years in which to learn how to be quiet.

choices.text: Sit across from him and ask the question
choices.consequence: You take the stool opposite and ask what he has been doing, and he says reading, mostly. He does not ask what you have been doing. He has already watched all of it happen.

nodes.text: The clerk runs it like a conference. Coffee with Henry at nine in the east room. Lunch with David at twelve on the terrace. Afternoon free, journaling encouraged, pens provided at the desk. There is a printed itinerary with your name across the header and a small map of the grounds. It is the strangest interview of your life, and you are somehow both the panel and the prize.

choices.text: Take the journaling seriously
choices.consequence: You fill nine pages before lunch, and the handwriting starts out as yours at thirty and finishes as yours at seventy. Whatever the pens are made of, they will not let you lie.

choices.text: Skip the journal — trust your gut
choices.consequence: You leave the pages blank and walk the corridors instead, and your gut says both, loudly, all afternoon. Instinct is not an answer here. It is only the question at higher volume.

nodes.text: There is a path between the hotel and a cliff, groomed like a golf course, with benches at intervals. Both men walk it with you, separately, an hour apart, and both ask about the parts they missed. David wants to know about your children, their names, their faces, everything. Henry wants to know about the spring you nearly left him, and he asks like a man who rehearsed it.

choices.text: Tell Henry the truth about that year
choices.consequence: You tell him you packed a case in March and unpacked it in April, and exactly why. He nods slowly at the sea. Forty years of not asking gets spent in one afternoon.

choices.text: Tell David about your children gently
choices.consequence: You describe your daughter's laugh and your son's enormous hands, and you watch a boy of twenty-three be genuinely glad about a life that only happened because he died.

nodes.text: There is a room here that will replay any day you lived, in whatever company you ask for. You step in alone first, only to test it, and land at nineteen in a college diner with a chipped Formica counter: David on one side, Henry's friend Walter on the other, all three of you laughing at something whose beginning you can no longer hear.

choices.text: Replay your wedding to Henry
choices.consequence: You stand at the back of your own wedding reception and watch yourself dance badly and mean every step of it. Fifty years starts here. You had forgotten how certain you were.

choices.text: Replay the night before David died
choices.consequence: You go back to the last ordinary evening, knowing exactly what the morning does, and you cannot alter one word of it. The room replays. It does not negotiate or take requests.

nodes.text: The clerk mentions it while stacking cups, as though it were a parking arrangement. You may also choose somebody still living. They will not be told. They will simply arrive one day, whenever that day turns out to be, and find you already waiting. Your daughter, for instance. Your oldest friend. He says it lightly and then leaves the room slightly too quickly.

choices.text: Consider waiting for your daughter
choices.consequence: You do the arithmetic of her remaining lifetime, forty years, maybe fifty, and discover you are willing. That willingness frightens you considerably more than dying did.

choices.text: Discard the option as too sad for them
choices.consequence: You refuse to hand your daughter a debt she never agreed to carry. Protecting her costs you the only version of this where nobody in the family gets left behind.

nodes.text: They let you watch, invisibly, the way you would watch weather through a window. Your daughter stands at the sink eating a sandwich over the plughole, and halfway through it she starts crying and goes on eating. Your son telephones his sister for the first time in fourteen months and neither of them mentions the gap. Your funeral flowers are on the kitchen table, going over.

choices.text: Stay and watch them for hours
choices.consequence: You stand in the corner of your own kitchen until it gets dark, learning things about your children you have no right to know. Watching costs nothing and it costs a great deal.

choices.text: Step back — they deserve privacy
choices.consequence: You leave your daughter to cry over the sink by herself, which is what she would want and what you would want, and doing it takes everything you have got.

nodes.text: You ask the clerk what David has been doing for fifty years. Waiting, he says. Reading. Painting quite badly. Waiting. It turns out the waiting room is not a figure of speech at all: there is an actual corridor in this building, with actual chairs, and people sitting in it who have been sitting since before you were born. Several of them are still watching the door.

choices.text: Sit with David in his waiting room
choices.consequence: You take the chair next to his and look at what he has been looking at for fifty years: a door, a lamp, a bad seascape in a gilt frame. Ten minutes of it nearly breaks you.

choices.text: Ask Henry how he'd feel about you choosing David
choices.consequence: You ask your husband for permission and watch him go about giving it decently, which is unbearable. He says he would understand. He means it. That is the part you cannot bear.

nodes.text: Two rooms, one truth each. To Henry: that fifty years is a country with its own language and its own weather and you have no idea how a person emigrates. To David: that you kept on living and changed shape a dozen times while he did not, and that the woman he has been waiting for grew old and became somebody else, and that somebody is the one sitting here.

choices.text: Notice how Henry hears 'leaving'
choices.consequence: He catches the word emigrate and goes very still, then starts talking about the house, the boiler, the garden, anything at all with a lock on it. He is arguing with a suitcase.

choices.text: Notice how David hears 'changed'
choices.consequence: He hears that you grew and he did not, and nods too quickly, agreeing with his own obsolescence. Nobody should ever agree that fast to having been outgrown.

nodes.text: It arrives at four in the morning, hotel-quiet: you want both. Not in sequence, not fairly, not as a compromise. Both, at once, the entire time. You want to be twenty-three on a porch and seventy in a kitchen, and you want a man in a cream blazer to produce a form that covers it. There is no such form. You go through the folder twice looking for it.

choices.text: Tell the clerk you want a third option
choices.consequence: You ask for the thing that does not exist, out loud, at four in the morning, in a lobby with nobody in it. The clerk does not laugh. He asks you to sit down.

choices.text: Resign yourself to choosing
choices.consequence: You accept that one of them has to lose, and for about an hour the acceptance feels like maturity, and then it stops feeling like anything except grief in a good coat.

nodes.text: Off the record, he says, and he actually says off the record, in the afterlife. There is a shared arrangement for souls in your precise bind. It is rare. It is not in the folder and it is not advertised anywhere. It needs all three of you to agree, and then to keep agreeing, and it asks for a kind of sharing most people discover they cannot manage once the door shuts.

choices.text: Propose the shared eternity
choices.consequence: You decide to ask two men to divide something neither of them has ever wanted divided. If they agree it will be because they love you, not because the arrangement is fair.

choices.text: Refuse — fairness is not a banquet
choices.consequence: You turn down the loophole because you can already see the arithmetic of it: whose birthday, whose evening, whose turn at the table. Some kindnesses are cruelty spread thinner.

nodes.text: You sit down with hotel paper to write your daughter something she will never receive. It runs to nine pages and takes the whole night, and the first line of it reads: I chose well. You look at that sentence for a long time with the pen resting on the blotter. You have not chosen anything yet, and you have already told her it turned out fine.

choices.text: Address it to whoever you choose
choices.consequence: You leave the name blank at the top and keep writing anyway, which means the letter has quietly become a promise you now have to go downstairs and make true.

choices.text: Address it to both Henry and David
choices.consequence: You put both names on one envelope and feel the impossibility of it arrive in your wrist. The pen carries on regardless. It always did know more than the rest of you.

nodes.text: Morning, and the lobby is emptier than it has been all week. The clerk has the folder open at the last page with a pen laid across it at a careful angle. He has done this thousands of times and he is, you can see it in the set of his jaw, quietly hoping for one particular outcome. He does not say which one. It would not be proper.

choices.text: Choose Henry — for the life you finished
choices.consequence: You choose the fifty years: the boiler, the ferry story told wrong, the hand on your back at every funeral the two of you ever attended together. You choose the life that got lived.

choices.text: Choose David — for the life you didn't get
choices.consequence: You choose the spring that never happened, knowing you are stepping back into a younger and smaller version of yourself to do it. Nobody else can go and collect that one.

choices.text: Choose the shared eternity, if both agree
choices.consequence: You ask two men to share what people do not share. The clerk writes it into the folder very slowly, as though the ink might raise an objection partway through.

choices.text: Choose to wait for your daughter
choices.consequence: You choose the person who is still alive and still eating sandwiches over a sink, and sign up for decades of an empty chair. It is the least romantic love in the building.

nodes.text: Whatever you decide, there is a room for the leaving. It is small, two chairs and a lamp that somebody thought hard about. The clerk waits in the corridor with the door not quite shut, close enough to be reached and far enough to be decent. Whoever you are not taking sits down opposite you. There is no clock in here, which is either mercy or the exact opposite.

choices.text: Tell each of them everything you'd want them to keep
choices.consequence: You give it all: the ferry, the porch, the year you nearly left, the corner turned down at page ninety. It takes hours and it empties you out properly.

choices.text: Keep it brief — feeling is enough
choices.consequence: You say one short true thing and stop, because past a certain length a goodbye starts serving the person who is leaving. You walk out with the rest of it still inside you.

nodes.text: The door opens onto a garden made of every good morning of fifty years stitched into one. The kettle is already on. He has the paper folded to the crossword with a single clue left, the way he always saved you one. He looks up and grins. You took your time, he says. Forgiven, he says, and then says it again, because he could never manage to say it only once.

choices.text: Stay in the morning, forever
choices.consequence: You sit down at the table and let the morning begin again, and again. You do not get bored of it. That, it turns out, is the whole of the miracle they were selling.

choices.text: Send a thought back to David, in mercy
choices.consequence: Before you sit down you ask the clerk to make sure the boy is not left alone in that corridor. It costs you nothing and it is the only reason you can enjoy the coffee.

nodes.text: He puts the book down without marking his place, for the first time in fifty years. The two of you walk out of the lobby into an April that never occurred: the rented flat on Sycamore with the temperamental boiler, the plan made on a cold porch. The years you actually lived are behind you now, shut and locked, and the key is somewhere you have agreed not to look.

choices.text: Live the spring forever
choices.consequence: You walk into the unlived April and let it be small: one street, one flat, one man reading aloud in a kitchen while you burn the onions. Small is what you were owed.

choices.text: Send your love back to Henry, in thanks
choices.consequence: You send fifty years of gratitude backwards down a line that is not built to carry it, and somehow it goes through. That is the last thing you will ever spend on him.

nodes.text: The clerk shows you into a room with two couches and a low table, and both men are already there holding mugs he handed them ten minutes ago. Neither has drunk anything. They look at each other for a long time, the boy who died at twenty-three and the man who buried you at seventy-four, and neither one of them looks away. Then, almost together, they look at you.

choices.text: Walk into the new shape of forever
choices.consequence: You cross the room and sit down between them, which is the least dignified and most honest thing you have ever done in your life. Nobody spills anything.

choices.text: Walk back to your own room and reconsider
choices.consequence: Your nerve goes at the threshold and you climb back upstairs, leaving two men holding cooling mugs on facing couches. You will have to walk into that room again from the beginning.

nodes.text: You take the tower room with the good window and tell the clerk that you will wait. Below, the years go past like a kind of weather. Henry arrives eventually, and after a long while goes off somewhere with David, and you hear about it secondhand. You are alone in the good sense: a woman keeping a chair warm, watching a door, with one arrival on her calendar.

choices.text: Wait for her, however long it takes
choices.consequence: You settle in for decades with no guarantee of the date and no way of hurrying it. Every single morning you check the lobby. It is the most patient thing you have ever done.

choices.text: Visit her each anniversary in dreams
choices.consequence: You ask for one night a year and are granted it, and spend the other three hundred and sixty-four hoping the dream lands somewhere useful in her head.

nodes.text: The morning runs again and it does not wear out, because it is the one you picked on purpose. Burnt toast. Coffee he makes badly and has always made badly. The crossword clue left for you in the margin. Somewhere around the thousandth repetition you understand that eternity is not a length at all but a thing you would agree to again, and you would agree to this, without needing to be asked.

You took Henry, and you made certain David was not left sitting in that corridor. The clerk arranged company for him: a woman who loved him in a life you will never hear a word about, who had been waiting in a different wing since long before you arrived. Nobody should be alone in forever. You believe that now with the particular force of somebody who nearly made an exception.

You live the April you were promised, and the surprise is that fifty unlived years do weigh something. You feel them in the doorway of the Sycamore flat most evenings, around the time the light goes. But they weigh less than one afternoon of him reading aloud while you burn the onions and swear at the pan. Forever turns out to be one street long. That is the whole of its kindness.

You find a way to get it to him. Not a letter, not a visit: a feeling in a supermarket car park, a line in a song on the radio that was not in the song a second earlier. Henry sits with both hands on the wheel and cries and cannot account for it. He will put it down to the weather, or the anniversary, or nothing. You know better than that.

It is strange, and it works, mostly. Henry and David never become friends exactly; they become something without a proper word for it, two men who split the same person and mind it less with every decade. There is a third mug now, and an ongoing argument about the crossword, and the clerk drops by on slow afternoons. Eternity is more flexible than the folder suggested. You simply have to ask out loud.

Decades. Then the lobby doors go and a grey-haired woman comes through holding a gold folder, and she is seventy years old and she has your hands exactly. She looks up at the tower window and laughs the laugh she got from you, unchanged. The clerk permits himself a small smile. You come down the stairs at an ordinary walking pace, because for the first time in your life there is no hurry.

You go to her the way her grandmother came to you: once a year, near dawn, in a dream she will half remember over breakfast and not quite be able to describe. She wakes up calmer. She is kinder to her husband for a week afterwards and cannot say why. You keep the tower chair, and the window, and the year between visits, and you learn that forever is mostly made of patience.
